name: Trazodone / prescription sleep meds

lead: Trazodone is a prescription antidepressant that doctors commonly prescribe off-label at low doses for insomnia. In sleep-optimization discussions it is a medical route to longer, more consolidated sleep, which people link to better recovery, skin and a fresher face.

It blocks serotonin 5-HT2A receptors and acts on adrenergic and histamine receptors, which is where its sedation is attributed. Systematic reviews, including a Cochrane review, report short-term gains in subjective sleep quality and fewer night-time awakenings, with low-to-moderate quality evidence and no long-term data; the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2017 guideline recommended against its use for insomnia. No study has examined it for appearance.

paras: It is taken in the evening under a doctor's prescription, usually as part of an insomnia treatment plan alongside sleep habits. Sleep effects are typically noticed within the first nights of use.

Reported adverse effects include dry mouth, sedation, headache, orthostatic hypotension and, rarely, QT prolongation, priapism, mania and liver toxicity. It is prescription-only in the US, UK, Canada and Australia, and stopping abruptly can cause a discontinuation syndrome.

angle.text: Trazodone is a prescription antidepressant widely used off-label to get longer, steadier sleep, which people link to better recovery, skin and a more rested face. Reviews have found short-term improvements in subjective sleep quality.

lead: Trazodone is a prescription antidepressant of the serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor class. It was developed by Angelini Research Laboratories in Italy in the 1960s, marketed in Italy from 1972, and approved by the US FDA in 1981 [1]. Its labelled use is major depressive disorder, but at lower doses it is widely prescribed off-label for insomnia [1].

In the looksmaxxing and recovery context, trazodone and other prescription sleep medicines are discussed as a medical route to better sleep, on the reasoning that sleep quality influences skin, body composition and overall appearance. No published study has examined trazodone for any appearance outcome.

Systematic reviews, including a Cochrane review, have reported short-term improvements in subjective sleep quality and fewer night-time awakenings, with low-to-moderate quality evidence and no data on long-term use. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2017 guideline recommended against its use for insomnia [1].

paras: The primary approved use is major depressive disorder. Off-label uses include anxiety disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder and obsessive-compulsive disorder, where evidence is limited, and it is often combined with SSRIs [1].

For insomnia, low doses are commonly prescribed off-label [1]. Other prescription sleep medicines discussed alongside it include Z-drugs such as zolpidem and orexin receptor antagonists such as daridorexant.

Common effects reported include dry mouth, faintness, vomiting, headache and sedation. Serious but less common effects include suicidal ideation (monitoring is advised in young people), mania, irregular heart rhythm or QT prolongation, and priapism. Orthostatic hypotension raises fall risk in older adults, and abrupt cessation can cause a discontinuation syndrome [1].

Trazodone is a potent 5-HT2A antagonist, a weaker 5-HT2C antagonist and a 5-HT1A partial agonist. It also blocks alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, weakly blocks histamine H1 receptors and weakly inhibits serotonin reuptake. It lacks anticholinergic activity [1].
Oral bioavailability is about 63 to 80 percent. The immediate-release half-life is about 4 to 15 hours. It is metabolised mainly by CYP3A4, CYP2D6 and CYP1A2 into an active metabolite, mCPP [1].

No studies have examined trazodone or other prescription sleep medicines for appearance outcomes. For insomnia itself, a Cochrane review and other systematic reviews reported short-term benefit for subjective sleep quality, with low-to-moderate quality evidence and no long-term data [1].

Registered trials include a 1,200-person phase 4 trial comparing common prescription and over-the-counter insomnia medications, recruiting from 2026 [2], and a 1,000-person phase 4 trial comparing digital therapy, trazodone and daridorexant for menopause-related insomnia, also recruiting [3]. Results have not been published.
Trazodone is prescription-only in the US, Canada, the UK and Australia. Brand names include Desyrel and Trittico worldwide, Molipaxin in the UK and Ireland, and Oleptro in the US [1].
